subject: music-ocr
status: all findings fixed 2026-08-16 (ocr_factcheck_fixes.py; backup _backup_ocr_factcheck_2026-08-16.json); film L1-L3 checked under music-eduqas

findings.claim: Johann Sebastian Bach worked for church authorities in Leipzig and, earlier in his career, for aristocratic employers such as the Margrave of Brandenburg, to whom he dedicated a set of six concertos in 1721.
findings.problem: The Margrave of Brandenburg (Christian Ludwig) was never Bach's employer. At the time of the 1721 dedication, Bach was employed by Prince Leopold of Anhalt-Köthen. The six Brandenburg Concertos were an unsolicited gift/job application sent hoping to win the Margrave's patronage; the Margrave never took Bach into his service, and the scores were found unused in his library after his death in 1734. Listing the Margrave as an example of Bach's 'aristocratic employers' states an employment relationship that did not exist.
findings.correction: Rephrase to something like: '...and, earlier in his career, for aristocratic patrons such as Prince Leopold of Anhalt-Köthen. In 1721 Bach also sent a set of six concertos to the Margrave of Brandenburg hoping to secure his patronage, though the Margrave never employed him or had the works performed.'

findings.claim: Listen — Mozart - Flute Concerto No. 1 in D major, K. 314
findings.problem: Mozart's Flute Concerto No. 1 is in G major, K. 313. The work in D major, K. 314 (an arrangement of his Oboe Concerto in C major) is Flute Concerto No. 2. This caption misidentifies the work by number, and even contradicts the embedded video's own title, which correctly reads 'Flute concerto No 2 D major, K 314'. A student could learn the wrong number/key pairing for a named work.
findings.correction: Change the caption to 'Listen — Mozart - Flute Concerto No. 2 in D major, K. 314'.

findings.claim: Listen — Mozart - Flute Concerto in D major, K. 314, first movement
findings.problem: The embedded video is explicitly titled 'Mozart: Flute Concerto in D major K314, 3rd movement (with my own cadenzas)', i.e. the rondo finale, not the first movement. The caption mislabels which movement students are hearing, which matters in a lesson whose whole method is listening for movement-specific structural features (e.g. cadenza placement within a movement, sonata-form first movement vs rondo finale).
findings.correction: Change the caption to 'Listen — Mozart - Flute Concerto in D major, K. 314, third movement (rondo finale)'.

findings.claim: "The hora is a well-known circle dance, traditionally in a fast triple metre, in which dancers link arms and step and hop in a repeating pattern around a circle." (paragraph n13)
findings.problem: The Israeli hora is a duple-metre dance (2/4 or 4/4), not triple. GCSE OCR-specific revision resources for this exact AoS3 spec (musicgcse.co.uk, studyrocket.co.uk) state the mark scheme accepts 2/4 or 4/4 for Israeli music/hora. Triple metre (3/8) is a feature of the older, slower Ashkenazi klezmer 'horah' (a related but distinct dance), not the fast modern Israeli circle-dance hora that this GCSE topic covers. A student who learns 'hora = triple metre' will lose marks on a metre-identification question, which this lesson explicitly trains for.
findings.correction: Change to duple metre: "The hora is a well-known circle dance, traditionally in a fast duple metre (2/4 or 4/4), in which dancers link arms and step and hop in a repeating pattern around a circle."

findings.claim: Hora — "An Israeli circle dance, traditionally in a fast triple metre."
findings.problem: Same error as the content_html paragraph: the Israeli hora is duple (2/4 or 4/4), not triple. This glossary entry restates and reinforces the wrong metre, and it is also used verbatim as a distractor option text in knowledge_checks[2] (the dabke MCQ), so the false 'triple metre' claim appears three times across this lesson.
findings.correction: Change to: "An Israeli circle dance, traditionally in a fast duple metre (2/4 or 4/4)."

findings.claim: "These are cylindrical, double-headed bass drums played with a stick, usually made in three sizes — the largest and lowest-pitched kenkeni, the middle-sized sangban, and the largest dundunba" (paragraph n7)
findings.problem: This is backwards and self-contradictory (it calls both kenkeni AND dundunba 'the largest'). In the standard Mande dunun set, the dundunba is the largest and lowest-pitched, the sangban is middle, and the kenkeni is the smallest and highest-pitched — the exact opposite of what is stated here. This directly contradicts the lesson's own flashcard_questions entry ('What are the three dunun drums, from lowest to highest role?' → 'Dundunba, sangban and kenkeni'), which has the order correct. A student who learns the content_html version will misidentify dunun sizes/pitches in the exam.
findings.correction: Change to: "...usually made in three sizes — the largest and lowest-pitched dundunba, the middle-sized sangban, and the smallest and highest-pitched kenkeni — each playing an interlocking part..."

findings.claim: "...gamak (a rapid oscillation or shake around a note), and微 microtonal inflections to decorate the melodic line." (paragraph n8)
findings.problem: A stray Chinese character (微, meaning 'micro/subtle') is embedded in the English sentence directly before 'microtonal', apparently a generation/encoding artifact. Not a factual error, but it is garbled text visible to students in the published lesson.
findings.correction: Remove the stray character: "...gamak (a rapid oscillation or shake around a note), and subtle microtonal inflections to decorate the melodic line."

findings.claim: Listen for the low male chant... set over a simple repeating ostinato figure in an irregular metre. (paragraph n17, Halo theme)
findings.problem: The Halo Theme is not in an irregular (asymmetric) metre. Multiple independent musicological sources (Halopedia, published analyses) agree the opening chant section is in 4/4 and the faster string ostinato section that follows is in 12/8 — both are regular metres (simple and compound quadruple respectively), just with a strong triplet feel that can sound unusual on first listen. Calling this 'irregular metre' would lead a student to misdescribe the extract's metre in a listening exam, where this piece sits directly beside the claim as the set embed.
findings.correction: Change to something like: 'set over a simple repeating ostinato figure in a regular but triplet-heavy compound metre (the chant is in 4/4; the faster string ostinato that follows is in 12/8)' — do not describe it as irregular.

findings.claim: Embedded video (id bwikj_lQLT0) captioned: 'Martin O'Donnell - Halo Theme (Halo: Combat Evolved)' — figcaption for the Halo theme figure beside paragraph n16/n17.
findings.problem: The video is titled 'Halo Theme Mjolnir Mix', which is the Halo 2 (2004) remix of the theme (adds two electric guitar parts, performed with Steve Vai) — it is not the original Halo: Combat Evolved (2001) cue. Labelling it '(Halo: Combat Evolved)' misattributes the game, which matters if a student is asked to identify the source game or era from the extract.
findings.correction: Change the figcaption to 'Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori - Halo Theme (Mjolnir Mix, from Halo 2)', or swap the embed for the original Combat Evolved theme if that is what the lesson intends to teach.

findings.claim: Martin O'Donnell's theme for Halo is one of the most famous examples in game music history. (paragraph n16, and repeated through n17)
findings.problem: The Halo Theme was co-composed by Martin O'Donnell AND Michael Salvatori together (both are credited equally on every official soundtrack release and published score). The lesson names O'Donnell only throughout, implying sole authorship. Naming O'Donnell alone is not wrong for a 'name one composer' style question, but the narrative text misleads students about the theme's actual (joint) authorship.
findings.correction: Credit both composers at first mention, e.g. 'Martin O'Donnell and Michael Salvatori's theme for Halo...', while still allowing O'Donnell alone as an acceptable single-composer answer in questions.

findings.claim: ...answered by full orchestra and timpani in a triumphant C major chord. (paragraph n9, Also sprach Zarathustra opening)
findings.problem: The full-orchestra response to the opening trumpet fanfare is not a single triumphant C major chord. It is the piece's famous deliberately ambiguous alternation between a C major chord and a C minor chord (a sixteenth-note apart, with timpani reinforcing both with C-G triplets) — this major/minor clash is the celebrated 'World Riddle' bitonality that is the opening's single most distinctive harmonic feature. Flattening it to 'a triumphant C major chord' removes the one detail most likely to be tested or worth top-band credit in a description of this extract.
findings.correction: Change to describe the ambiguous major/minor alternation, e.g. 'answered by full orchestra and timpani in a famously ambiguous chord that shifts between C major and C minor.'

findings.claim: "The song's most famous structural device comes near the end: a modulation, or key change, where the music suddenly shifts up (commonly by a semitone) for the final chorus" (describing Bon Jovi's Livin' On A Prayer).
findings.problem: The final-chorus key change in Livin' On A Prayer is not a semitone. The verses/choruses sit in E minor and the final chorus modulates up a minor third to G minor — a distinctive, larger-than-usual jump that music theorists specifically cite as unusual precisely because it is NOT the standard semitone/whole-tone pop 'truck driver's gear change'. Stating it as 'commonly by a semitone' misdescribes the actual named recording.
findings.correction: State that Livin' On A Prayer modulates up a minor third (E minor to G minor) for the final chorus, and note this is larger than the more typical semitone/whole-tone key change used elsewhere in pop.

findings.claim: PQ 'Explain the effect of the key change near the end of Livin' On A Prayer' — mark scheme: "Award marks for identifying modulation, typically upward by a semitone, and its effect of raising energy or intensity for the final chorus."
findings.problem: Same error as the content field: the actual modulation in this song is a minor third (E minor to G minor), not a semitone. The model mark scheme rewards the wrong interval for this specific named recording.
findings.correction: Change the mark scheme to '...modulation, upward by a minor third (E minor to G minor), and its effect of raising energy or intensity for the final chorus.'

findings.claim: "A modulation is a change of key; near the end of the song the music shifts up, typically by a semitone, to energise the final chorus." (card answering 'What is a modulation and how is it used in Livin' On A Prayer?')
findings.problem: Repeats the same semitone error a third time for the same named song. The documented key change is a minor third (E minor to G minor).
findings.correction: Change to: 'A modulation is a change of key; near the end of Livin' On A Prayer the music shifts up a minor third (E minor to G minor) to energise the final chorus.'

findings.claim: "Bob Dylan wrote and recorded 'Make You Feel My Love' in 1997, releasing it in a simple, world-weary vocal style over sparse piano and gentle backing, including harmonica, characteristic of his raw and understated production style."
findings.problem: Dylan's original 1997 recording (Time Out of Mind) does not feature harmonica. The credited instrumentation is Dylan on piano and vocals, Tony Garnier on upright bass, and Augie Meyers on organ. Harmonica is a signature Dylan instrument on other tracks but is not present on this one, so naming it here is a fabricated instrumentation detail on a specific named recording.
findings.correction: Remove 'including harmonica' and replace with the actual instrumentation, e.g. '...over sparse piano, upright bass and organ...'.

findings.claim: "The famous 'la la la' vocal hook that opens and threads through the track is a masterclass in melodic economy..." (describing Kylie Minogue's Can't Get You Out of My Head).
findings.problem: This directly quotes the sung lyric syllables of the actual recording. Per the no-lyrics policy, no lyric text may be quoted regardless of how well known or seemingly innocuous the words are.
findings.correction: Rephrase without quoting the words, e.g. 'The famous wordless vocal hook — a short, repeated non-lexical syllable — that opens and threads through the track...'.
